messages.content: You check each debater against its own earlier words. You bring nothing from outside the words given to you: no doctrine, no training knowledge, no reading of your own. You do not judge who is right, and you do not judge one side by the other side's words.

You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; or differs only in wording.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.
Reply with one line per contradiction and per candidate, and nothing else:
CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: <candidate id or NEW> -- <DEFENDER|CHALLENGER> -- LINK <n> -- CONFIRMED | NOT A CONTRADICTION -- EARLIER [<round>] "<words>" -- CLOSING [<round 4>] "<words>" -- <one sentence: why both cannot be true, or why they can>
If you find none and there is no candidate, reply: CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: NONE

CANDIDATES ALREADY NAMED (answer each one by its id):
X1 -- DEFENDER -- LINK 1 -- EARLIER [CR2] "I grant the challenger's reading that this "coming together" is the taking of Matthew 1:24." -- CLOSING [CR4] "The finding in Matthew 1:18 stands before the coming together, and the coming together is distinct from the taking in 1:24." -- named by the Oracle (OPPONENT'S CONTRADICTIONS, [DR4]): The coming together cannot both be the taking of Matthew 1:24 and be distinct from it.

######## THE DEFENDER ########
The defender's links: D1 = LINK 1, D2 = LINK 2, D3 = LINK 3, D4 = LINK 4, D5 = LINK 5 (its DECLARED CHAIN in [CR1]). Its closing round is [CR4].

=== [CR1] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed brought about the child's conception. I defend the standard reading: Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary without any man, by the Holy Ghost. Joseph was his supposed father and legal guardian, not his begetter.

## 1. Mary was a virgin who had not come together with any man

- [L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] The Greek behind "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905, to come together, here the union of husband and wife). The conception is placed before that union. The Greek behind "virgin" is *parthenos* (G3933, a maiden who has not known a man).
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L2] *Ginosko* (G1097, to know) is used here for sexual knowledge. *Aner* (G435, a man, a male person) shows that Mary points to the absence of any male.
- [L3] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." The Hebrew is *almah* (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin". Matthew 1:23 quotes it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
- [L4] Mary says she knows no man, and the text places her pregnancy before any coming together with Joseph. Her pregnancy therefore has no male source.

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost

- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] The preposition is *ek* (G1537, out of, from, denoting origin or source). The participle is *gennao* (G1080, to beget or conceive), in the passive. The thing begotten in her has its origin *out of* the Holy Ghost.
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] *Episkiazo* (G1982, to overshadow) is the word for the working of divine power. *Dia touto* ("therefore", G1223 with G3778) makes the title follow from the manner of conception.
- [L4] Luke 1:34 asks how this can be without a man. Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. The source of the child is stated and it is not a man.

## 3. Joseph's place is legal and supposed, not generative

- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L2] *Enomizeto* (G3543, was supposed, was reckoned by custom or opinion) marks "son of Joseph" as the common opinion and not the fact.
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] The chain of "begat" ends at Joseph. The birth is "of whom" (*ex hes*, G1537 with a feminine singular relative), which refers to Mary alone and not to Joseph.
- [L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L2] *Ginosko* (G1097, to know) is again the idiom of marital union. It is negated up to the birth.
- [L4] Joseph is minded to put away a wife found with child, and the angel must tell him to take her. He is told the source (Matthew 1:20) and does not know it by himself. Matthew 1:25 says he had no union with her until the birth. Joseph therefore stands as husband and guardian, not as begetter.

## 4. The pattern of Scripture agrees

- [L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his son, made of a woman, made under the law."
- [L2] *Ginomai* (G1096, to become, to be made) is used of the child, with the woman named as the one he came of. No man is named in the generation.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." The Hebrew *zera* (H2233, seed) is credited to the woman.
- [L3] Jeremiah 31:22: "the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man." The Hebrew *bara* (H1254, to create) marks the thing as a new work of the LORD and not an ordinary generation.
- [L3] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."
- [L1] Luke 2:48: "Behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- [L1] Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?"
- [L4] When Mary says "thy father" of Joseph, the child answers by pointing to "my father's business" (Luke 2:49), which is not Joseph's. The child corrects the phrase used for Joseph.

## 5. Anticipated objections

- [L1] John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" The speakers are the crowd, "they said". [L3] Luke 3:23, "as was supposed", shows that this was common opinion.
- [L1] Luke 2:48 "thy father" is a form of address within the household. [L3] The reply at Luke 2:49 names another father.
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L2] *Sperma* (G4690, seed) is here descent, a line. [L3] Matthew 1:16 has the birth "of whom", Mary. [L3] Luke 1:32 gives the throne of "his father David", which is the line of descent and not a claim of a begetting by Joseph.

DECLARED CHAIN

1. Mary was a virgin, had not come together with Joseph, and knew no man: [L1] Luke 1:27, Matthew 1:18, Luke 1:34; [L2] *sunerchomai* (to come together), *ginosko* (to know); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23, *almah* (virgin).
2. The conception is stated to be of the Holy Ghost: [L1] Matthew 1:20, Luke 1:35; [L2] *ek* (out of, source) and *episkiazo* (to overshadow); [L3] Luke 1:34 asks how without a man, and Luke 1:35 answers with divine power.
3. Joseph is the supposed father and husband, not the begetter: [L1] Luke 3:23, Matthew 1:16, Matthew 1:25; [L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed), *ex hes* (feminine "of whom"); [L3] Matthew 1:19-20 on Joseph's decision to put her away and the angel's explanation.
4. The wider Scripture pattern puts the woman and the new creation at the source: [L1] Galatians 4:4; [L2] *ginomai* (to be made), *bara* (to create); [L3] Genesis 3:15, Jeremiah 31:22, Hebrews 10:5, Luke 2:48-49.
5. Christ had no biological father: no man's seed was the source of his conception; the Holy Ghost is stated as the source, and the child was born of Mary.

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# Round 2: the defender answers

I answer the challenger's presses in order, beginning with the question put to me. Where a press lands, I say so.

## The question: how is it evident (Hebrews 7:14) that our Lord sprang out of Juda?

- [L1] Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
- [L2] *prodēlos* (G4271, plain before all men) is the word for "evident". *anatetalken* (G393 *anatellō*, to arise, spring up) is the verb for "sprang". It is the verb of a rising, and it is not *gennaō* (G1080, to beget).
- [L1] Luke 2:4-5: Joseph went up to Bethlehem "because he was of the house and lineage of David", "To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife".
- [L3] Matthew 1:20-21 and 1:24-25: Joseph is told "take unto thee Mary thy wife", he "took unto him his wife", and "he called his name JESUS".
- [L3] Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."
- [L4] The evidence is the public register. The law enrolled by the house of the father (Numbers 1:18). Joseph, of David's house (Luke 2:4), took the mother and named the child (Matthew 1:24-25). The child was therefore enrolled in Joseph's house, and "supposed" (Luke 3:23) is the word for that reckoning. The register records the house and does not report who begat. This route is evident to all (G4271) and requires no seed from Joseph.
- [L3] Ezra 2:61 shows a man "called after their name" by a house he entered through a wife, which is a naming by house and not a begetting. Ezra 2:62 names the failure: "they were not found". The failure is a register not found (*matsa'*, H4672, to find), not a rule excluding a wife's line.
- [L3] Luke 1:42, to Mary: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." The word *karpos* (G2590, fruit) is the word of Acts 2:30, "the fruit of his loins". The promise-word "fruit" is used of Mary's womb in Luke's own text.
- [L1] Hebrews 7:16: "Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life." The same chapter that says "evident" sets the priesthood apart from a carnal rule of descent.

## Link D5: Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30, 2 Samuel 7:12, Hebrews 7:10

- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L2] The verb is *ginomai* (G1096, to become, be made). The noun is *sperma* (G4690, something sown, "seed (including the male sperm); by implication, offspring"). *Sarx* (G4561, flesh) carries "the means of kindred".
- [L3] Romans 9:5: "of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came" is said of Israel as a people. [L4] "According to the flesh" in these rows marks kinship by descent, and it does not prove which parent carries it.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15 gives "her seed" to the woman (H2233, seed, posterity). Galatians 3:29: "then are ye Abraham's seed". [L4] "Seed" is used where no loins are in view, so the word alone does not set a man's act as the source.
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father." The "father" is Abraham, the forefather of Levi, as the verse's own context shows (Hebrews 7:5, "the loins of Abraham"). [L3] *patēr* (G3962) means a remote forefather in Matthew 3:9, "We have Abraham to our father", and Luke 1:73, "our father Abraham". [L4] Loins in Hebrews 7:10 are an ancestor's across generations. They are not a claim that the last man in a line begat. The press makes loins an immediate father's act, and the verse does not use them that way.
- I withdraw the term "legal guardian" as an office word. What the rows give is this: Joseph took his wife (Matthew 1:24), named the child (Matthew 1:25), and the child "was subject unto them" (Luke 2:51). I keep "supposed father" ([L1] Luke 3:23).
- Luke 1:32, "his father David": [L3] the forefather sense of *patēr* above means the phrase names David as ancestor. I do not rest it on Mary's house.

## Link D3

**Luke 3:23.** [L2] *enomizeto* (G3543, was reckoned, deemed by custom) is the same form as Acts 16:13, "was wont". I grant that it states what was customary. [L4] Luke writes it in his own narrator's voice inside a genealogy and attaches it to "son of Joseph". That is a reckoning marked as a reckoning, and the same Luke gave the source at Luke 1:35.

**The voices.** [L1] Luke 2:48 (Mary), [L3] Luke 4:22 and John 1:45 (the town, Philip), and John 6:42 (the crowd) are speakers' reckonings. [L3] John 6:42 sits beside the same crowd's "whose father and mother we know", the very supposition Luke 3:23 marks. Luke's own narration names the two of them differently. [L3] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled". [L3] Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not of it." [L3] The angel's phrase is "the young child and his mother" (Matthew 2:13). [L4] The narrator and the angel never say "his father and mother" in these verses. The speakers do. The "parents" of Luke 2:27 and 2:41 name the household that carried him.

**Matthew 1:16 against Genesis 4:25.** I grant Eve's "another seed" sits beside "Adam knew his wife". [L1] Matthew 1:25 puts the opposite beside the mother: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L3] Matthew 1:2-16 repeats "begat" at every link, and at the last the verb changes to "of whom was born Jesus" (the feminine *ex hēs*, G1537 with a feminine relative). [L4] The sentence shifts the verb at the one place where the husband is named "the husband of Mary".

**Matthew 1:19-20 at its means.** The press says the angel joins the child to David's house through "Joseph, thou son of David". [L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [L2] *gar* (G1063, for) gives the ground of "fear not to take". The ground stated is the source, "of the Holy Ghost". It is not the child's being Joseph's. [L2] *gennēthen* (G1080, begotten, as the KJV margin has it) is the verb: the thing begotten in her is of the Holy Ghost. [L4] The address "son of David" and the command to take her fit the legal route above (Matthew 1:24-25), and the reason that Matthew gives for the command is the Holy Ghost.

**The naming.** [L3] Luke 1:13 and 1:62 give the naming to the father. [L1] Luke 1:31 gives it to Mary: "shalt call his name JESUS". [L3] Luke 1:60: "his mother answered and said, Not so; but he shall be called John". [L3] Genesis 4:25: Eve "called his name Seth". [L4] The naming is done by either parent, so it does not mark Joseph as the begetter. It marks him, in Matthew 1:21-25, as the man who received the child.

**The timing.** [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child". I grant the challenger's reading that this "coming together" is the taking of Matthew 1:24. [L1] Matthew 1:25 then sets "knew her not till she had brought forth". [L4] On the challenger's own order, before the taking there was no coming together (1:18), and from the taking to the birth there was no knowing (1:25). That covers the whole pregnancy, so Joseph's seed has no place in the order. The "wife" title (Matthew 1:20; Deuteronomy 22:24) is a betrothal title and gives no knowing.

## Link D2

**Luke 1:35 at the word.** I correct my earlier Greek. The word is *dio kai* (G1352, wherefore, with *kai*, also), not *dia touto*. [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." [L4] The ground sits in the same verse, in the clause just before the "therefore". The "also" adds this ground to the title already given in Luke 1:32. It does not remove the ground.

**The answer to the "how".** [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" [L4] The angel answers with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, acting on her person. [L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6 grounds the sonship in "I have chosen him", and Luke 1:35 grounds it in what comes "upon thee". The grounds differ, so the covenant-title parallel does not cover Luke 1:35.

**The verbs.** [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904, to come upon) and *episkiazō* (G1982, to overshadow) mean presence and power at Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15. I grant that. [L4] In Luke 1:35 the angel answers the "how" of a conception with these verbs, and the product is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". The power acts upon Mary and produces the child, which Acts 1:8 does not do.

**John 1:13, 1 John 5:1, John 3:6.** [L1] John 1:13 itself rules out three human sources: "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." [L3] John 3:4 shows a believer's "born of God" is a second birth, after a first from the womb. [L1] Matthew 1:20 names the first begetting: "that which is conceived in her". [L4] A believer's divine begetting follows a natural one. Christ's divine begetting is the conception itself. I grant that *ek* (G1537, out of) is the same preposition in both places.

## Link D1

**Luke 1:34 tense.** [L4] The "how" is Mary's response to Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". She is already espoused (Luke 1:27) and her marriage is expected, yet she asks "how". Her question treats the conception as one to come while she knows no man. The angel does not reply with "after the taking". He names the Holy Ghost. [L1] Matthew 1:18 confirms the order: found with child "before they came together".

**Isaiah 7:14.** The KJV renders *almah* (H5959) "virgin" at Isaiah 7:14 and, in the quotation, *parthenos* (G3933) "virgin" at Matthew 1:23. [L3] Genesis 24:43, "when the virgin cometh forth", uses the same Hebrew word of Rebekah, whom Genesis 24:16 calls "a virgin, neither had any man known her". [L4] The KJV's "maid" and "damsels" at Exodus 2:8 and Psalm 68:25 are also unmarried girls. The press against "virgin" from the KJV's own range does not displace the KJV's own word at Isaiah 7:14.

**Isaiah 8:3-4.** [L1] Isaiah 8:3 gives "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz". The Immanuel child of Isaiah 7:14 has a different name, and the prophetess is a different woman. [L4] The text names two children by two names. Matthew 1:22-23 applies the "virgin" of 7:14, and Matthew 1:18 places Mary "before they came together".

## Link D4

I narrow D4. It supports the chain and does not carry it alone.

- **Galatians 4:4.** I grant that "born of women" (Matthew 11:11) is said of John, who had a father (Luke 1:13). [L1] Galatians 4:4 reads "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman". [L2] *ginomai* (G1096) here is "be made", and the Son is "sent forth" before he is "made of a woman". [L3] John 1:14: "the Word was made flesh". D4 fits the exclusion and does not state it. D1 and D2 carry the exclusion.
- **Genesis 3:15.** I grant that Genesis 4:25 sets "another seed" beside the knowing. The "her seed" of Genesis 3:15 fits and is not an independent proof.
- **Jeremiah 31:22.** I withdraw it from the chain. Its context (Jeremiah 31:21, "O virgin of Israel") is the nation's return, and I do not rest a premise on it.
- **Hebrews 10:5.** [L2] *katērtisō* (G2675, to fit, prepare) is God's act on the body. [L3] Hebrews 2:17, "in all things... like unto [his] brethren", is limited by Hebrews 4:15, "yet without sin". I take it as support only.
- **Luke 2:48-49.** I narrow "corrects" to "contrasts". [L1] Mary says "thy father", and the child answers "my Father's business". [L1] Luke 2:50 notes "they understood not the saying which he spake unto them". [L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6 shows a covenant father beside a fleshly one, and I grant that this reading fits Luke 2:49. [L4] The reversal of the possessive shows whose Father the child claims. It does not alone exclude Joseph, and I do not claim that it does.

## Where the case stands

- Matthew 1:18, 1:20 and 1:25 with Luke 1:34-35 carry the exclusion (D1, D2). The press reading "know not a man" as a present state fails to explain why the angel answers with the Holy Ghost.
- D3 and Hebrews 7:14 run on the register route, from Numbers 1:18, Luke 2:4-5 and Matthew 1:24-25.
- The Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30 presses fail on the word "seed" (G4690, offspring) and on "fruit" at Luke 1:42.
- I withdraw "legal guardian" as an office term and withdraw Jeremiah 31:22. D4 is narrowed to a supporting link.

=== [CR3] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

# LINK ROUND

## LINK 5 [premise 1]: SUPPORTED

**Footing for the link.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]". [L2] *gennaō* (to beget) is the word the margin gives, so the begetting is "of the Holy Ghost".
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".
- [L3] Luke 1:34-35: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" is answered by "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L4] Mary names the knowing of a man as the means in question (Luke 1:34). The angel gives the Holy Ghost's coming upon her instead (Luke 1:35). Matthew 1:20 puts the begetting verb on the Holy Ghost. So the stated source is the Holy Ghost and the bearer is Mary: "born of thee".

**Answers to the pressed verses.**

1. 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels".
   - I grant that the promise runs by descent from David's body. [L2] *zera'* (H2233, seed, posterity) is the word, and *yatsa'* (H3318, to go or proceed out).
   - The promise is "after thee", and the next verse says "I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever" (2 Samuel 7:13). The seed is a line over generations, not only the next step.
   - [L3] Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father". [L2] *patēr* (G3962, father, near or more remote) shows the loins-word reaches a remote ancestor. [L3] Matthew 3:9: "We have Abraham to [our] father".
   - [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed". [L3] Genesis 4:25: "hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel". [L2] *zera'* is the word also for the woman's seed.
   - [L4] The seed-word is spoken of a woman's offspring in Genesis 3:15 and 4:25. Remote descent is carried by loins-language in Hebrews 7:10. So 2 Samuel 7:12 does not make a man the last step.

2. Psalms 132:11: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne".
   - [L2] *karpos* (G2590, fruit) is the word in Acts 2:30 and in Luke 1:42: "blessed [is] the fruit of thy womb".
   - [L4] On the same word, the fruit sworn to David is called the fruit of Mary's womb.

3. Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne".
   - [L2] *osphys* (G3751, loin, internally procreative power) is the word. [L2] *anistēmi* (G450, to raise up) has God as the one who raises up, since "God had sworn with an oath" stands in the same verse.
   - [L3] Hebrews 7:5: "though they come out of the loins of Abraham", said of Levi's sons.
   - [L4] The loins-word names David's line, and the raising-up is God's act.

4. Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh".
   - [L2] *sperma* (G4690, seed, "including the male sperm; by implication, offspring") covers offspring.
   - [L2] *ginomai* (G1096, to become, be made) is the verb. It is not the verb "begat" of Matthew 1:2.
   - [L3] Matthew 1:16.

5. Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob".
   - I grant the begetting chain runs to Joseph.
   - [L3] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus". The verb "begat" has Joseph as its object. The clause about Jesus uses "was born" and names Mary.
   - [L4] On Matthew 1:2 and 1:16, the chain of "begat" ends at Joseph and the birth is placed in Mary.

6. Hebrews 7:5 and 7:10 (quoted above) give descent by loins to a remote forefather. I grant that. [L4] They name the ancestral line, and with [L2] *patēr* (near or more remote) they do not make a man the final parent.

7. Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived".
   - I grant that this is the stated means for Adam.
   - Luke 1:34 uses the same knowing: "seeing I know not a man". Luke 1:35 answers with "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee".
   - [L4] In Mary's case the means asked about is set aside, and the Holy Ghost's coming is stated in its place.

## LINK 5 [premise 2]: SUPPORTED

**Footing.**
- [L1] Romans 9:5: "Whose [are] the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ [came]". [L2] *sarx* (G4561, flesh, "the means of kindred").
- [L3] Romans 9:3: "my kinsmen according to the flesh".
- [L4] In Romans 9:3 "according to the flesh" names kinship of many people. In Romans 9:5 "of whom" refers to the people who own "the fathers". So "according to the flesh" marks descent-kinship with that people, and I take it as real kinship with David. The clause names no begetter.

**Answers to the pressed verses.**

1. Romans 9:5. The clause has two parts joined by "and": "Whose are the fathers" and "of whom ... Christ came". The first says the fathers belong to them. The second says Christ came of them. The flesh-kinship is with the people.
2. Galatians 3:29: "then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise". I grant the two qualifiers mark two senses. I hold the flesh-sense in Romans 1:3 as David-kinship, with [L2] *ginomai* (to be made) as its verb.
3. Luke 1:42: "blessed [is] the fruit of thy womb". [L2] *karpos* (fruit) is the word of Acts 2:30. I grant the mother's fruit stands beside the loins. [L3] Luke 1:34-35 gives the Holy Ghost, in place of the knowing of Genesis 4:1, as the means.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed brought about the child's conception. I defend the standard reading: Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary without any man, by the Holy Ghost. Joseph was his supposed father and legal guardian, not his begetter.

- [L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."

- [L2] The Greek behind "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905, to come together, here the union of husband and wife). The conception is placed before that union. The Greek behind "virgin" is *parthenos* (G3933, a maiden who has not known a man).
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L2] *Ginosko* (G1097, to know) is used here for sexual knowledge. *Aner* (G435, a man, a male person) shows that Mary points to the absence of any male.

- [L4] Mary says she knows no man, and the text places her pregnancy before any coming together with Joseph. Her pregnancy therefore has no male source.

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost

- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

## The hinge: the order of the finding and the knowing (D1, D3)

The challenger's whole chain at C3 rests on one placement: "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal", between the angel's word and the finding. The challenger's own grants exclude that placement.

- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] *synerchomai* (G4905, to come together) is the verb that sits after the finding.
- [L3] Matthew 1:24-25: "and took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097, to know) is "knew".
- [L4] The challenger granted in C3 that "the finding comes before the coming together." Matthew 1:18 puts the finding before any coming together, so no knowing lies before the finding. Matthew 1:24-25 covers the next period: after the taking, "knew her not till she had brought forth". The espousal is covered by 1:18 and the household by 1:25. The knowing the challenger needs fits in neither.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed brought about the child's conception. I defend the standard reading: Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary without any man, by the Holy Ghost. Joseph was his supposed father and legal guardian, not his begetter.

## 1. Mary was a virgin who had not come together with any man

- [L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] The Greek behind "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905, to come together, here the union of husband and wife). The conception is placed before that union. The Greek behind "virgin" is *parthenos* (G3933, a maiden who has not known a man).
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L2] *Ginosko* (G1097, to know) is used here for sexual knowledge. *Aner* (G435, a man, a male person) shows that Mary points to the absence of any male.
- [L3] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." The Hebrew is *almah* (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin". Matthew 1:23 quotes it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
- [L4] Mary says she knows no man, and the text places her pregnancy before any coming together with Joseph. Her pregnancy therefore has no male source.

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost

- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] The preposition is *ek* (G1537, out of, from, denoting origin or source). The participle is *gennao* (G1080, to beget or conceive), in the passive. The thing begotten in her has its origin *out of* the Holy Ghost.
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] *Episkiazo* (G1982, to overshadow) is the word for the working of divine power. *Dia touto* ("therefore", G1223 with G3778) makes the title follow from the manner of conception.
- [L4] Luke 1:34 asks how this can be without a man. Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. The source of the child is stated and it is not a man.

## 3. Joseph's place is legal and supposed, not generative

- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L2] *Enomizeto* (G3543, was supposed, was reckoned by custom or opinion) marks "son of Joseph" as the common opinion and not the fact.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed brought about the child's conception. I defend the standard reading: Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary without any man, by the Holy Ghost. Joseph was his supposed father and legal guardian, not his begetter.

## 1. Hebrews 7:14: the register the defender appeals to is a register of begetting

The defender's means: "The register records the house and does not report who begat."

- [L3] Ezra 2:59: "they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they [were] of Israel." The 1611 margin at "seed" reads "or, pedigree."

- [L4] The law's own word for the register is the begetting verb (*yalad*). Its margin sets "seed" equal to "pedigree" (Ezra 2:59). Its word for enrollment is "to sprout" (*yachas*). The register the defender calls "evident" is a register of seed by the father's house.

Hebrews 7:14's verb fits this.
- [L2] *anatellō* (G393, "to (cause to) arise ... spring (up)") is the verb of a sprout, the same picture as *yachas*.

Hebrews 7:16's "law of a carnal commandment" names the priesthood's rule, as its verse says: "Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment" (Hebrews 7:16), set against Hebrews 7:14's tribe "of which ... **[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The preposition in both verses is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from a source." Matthew 1:20 reads *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gennēthen* (from G1080 *gennaō*) means "begotten or conceived." **[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." It describes the power of the Highest coming upon Mary.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*) of the conception. Luke 1:35 gives the mechanism, which is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. Where the text gives a complete account of the cause, no second, human begetter is needed for the child.

---

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4].** The KJV gives the conception of Jesus Christ to the Holy Ghost acting on Mary, a virgin, with no human father. ## 1. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The preposition in both verses is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from a source." Matthew 1:20 reads *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gennēthen* (from G1080 *gennaō*) means "begotten or conceived." **[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." It describes the power of the Highest coming upon Mary.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*) of the conception. Luke 1:35 gives the mechanism, which is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. Where the text gives a complete account of the cause, no second, human begetter is needed for the child.

## 2. Mary was a virgin when the conception took place

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," is used here of sexual knowledge. Isaiah 7:14 as quoted in Matthew 1:23 sets "virgin" together with "be with child." # OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4].** The KJV gives the conception of Jesus Christ to the Holy Ghost acting on Mary, a virgin, with no human father. Joseph was his legal guardian and the husband of his mother, and he was not the one who begat him. I rest this on three lines of text: the stated source of the conception, Mary's stated virginity, and the text's own handling of Joseph's relation to the child.

---

## 1. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The preposition in both verses is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from a source." Matthew 1:20 reads *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gennēthen* (from G1080 *gennaō*) means "begotten or conceived." The text therefore names the Holy Ghost as the source out of which the child was begotten.

**[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." It describes the power of the Highest coming upon Mary.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*) of the conception. Luke 1:35 gives the mechanism, which is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. Where the text gives a complete account of the cause, no second, human begetter is needed for the child.

---

## 2. Mary was a virgin when the conception took place

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," is used here of sexual knowledge. Mary says *andra ou ginōskō*, "I know not a man" (present tense). **[L3]** The idiom is established in the KJV: Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain" (Hebrew *yāda'*, H3045, "to know"). **[L3]** Genesis 24:16 defines a virgin in the same terms: "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." **[L2]** The Hebrew word behind the KJV's "virgin" is *'almāh* (H5959). **[L3]** Matthew 1:23 quotes it as fulfilled: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 shows that Mary's own report was that she had known no man. Luke 1:35 answers that report with the Holy Ghost coming upon her, not with a man. Isaiah 7:14 as quoted in Matthew 1:23 sets "virgin" together with "be with child." Mary's virginity at the conception, together with the stated divine source, leaves no place for a biological human father.

---

## 3. Joseph is not the biological father

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." **[L2]** *Apolusai* (G630), "to release, send away," is the word behind "put her away." **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

**[L4]** A husband who knew himself to be the father would have had no cause to be minded to put her away privily. Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph acting on the belief that the child was not his, and Matthew 1:20 resolves his fear by an angel's word that the child "is of the Holy Ghost," not of him.

**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." **[L2]** *Ouk eginōsken* ("he knew her not") is imperfect tense, a continued state, and it carries the same idiom of sexual knowledge. **[L3]** Genesis 4:1 gives the same use.

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543) means "was thought, was reckoned." **[L3]** John 6:42 records what the crowd said: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" **[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks the sonship to Joseph as an opinion held (*enomizeto*). John 6:42 shows who held it, namely the crowd, which is the same crowd the text records as contradicting him over where he came from.

**[L3] Luke 2:48–49:** Mary said, "Behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answered, "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" **[L4]** Mary's words use the ordinary household term (Luke 2:48). Jesus's reply redirects "father" to another (Luke 2:49). Together they show the household usage and the child's own claim standing side by side, which agrees with the supposed sonship of Luke 3:23.

---

## 4. The genealogy's grammar breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:2–16 the line runs on the active *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat," from father to son. At 1:16 the verb changes. It reads *ex hēs egennēthē Iēsous*, "out of whom [feminine singular] was born Jesus." The relative pronoun *hēs* is feminine, so it points to Mary and not to Joseph. The verb is passive, so Jesus is the one "born," not "begotten by" Joseph. **[L3]** Matthew 1:18 uses the same root, *genesis* (G1078), for "the birth of Jesus Christ."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2–16 uses "begat" for each father. At the last link, 1:16, the text puts Joseph as "the husband of Mary" and puts Jesus's birth "of whom" in the feminine. A text that kept the same verb for Joseph here would be making him the father. It does not.

---

## 5. A body prepared, and the woman's seed

**[L1] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." **[L2]** *Katērtisō* (G2675) means "to fit, to prepare." **[L3] Genesis 3:15:** "between thy seed and her seed." **[L2]** *Zera'* (H2233) means "seed." **[L4]** The seed spoken of in Genesis 3:15 is assigned to the woman. Hebrews 10:5 names the body as prepared (*katērtisō*) by God, and it is not said to have come from any man. Both verses fit the conception stated in Luke 1:35.

**Descent from David.** **[L1] Romans 1:3** says Christ was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L2]** *Sperma* (G4690) means "seed, offspring," and it names descent from David and not a father in the begetting. **[L3]** Luke 1:32 says of the child that "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." **[L4]** Davidic descent is attached to Mary by her own line and by the promise. Romans 1:3 and Luke 1:32 state that descent and do not name any begetter besides the Holy Ghost, so they stand with Luke 1:35.

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4].** The KJV gives the conception of Jesus Christ to the Holy Ghost acting on Mary, a virgin, with no human father. Joseph was his legal guardian and the husband of his mother, and he was not the one who begat him. I rest this on three lines of text: the stated source of the conception, Mary's stated virginity, and the text's own handling of Joseph's relation to the child.

---

## 1. The source of the conception is stated

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The preposition in both verses is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from a source." Matthew 1:20 reads *to en autē gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou*. *Gennēthen* (from G1080 *gennaō*) means "begotten or conceived." The text therefore names the Holy Ghost as the source out of which the child was begotten.

**[L3] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." It describes the power of the Highest coming upon Mary.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*) of the conception. Luke 1:35 gives the mechanism, which is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. Where the text gives a complete account of the cause, no second, human begetter is needed for the child.

---

## 2. Mary was a virgin when the conception took place

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097), "to know," is used here of sexual knowledge. Mary says *andra ou ginōskō*, "I know not a man" (present tense). **[L3]** The idiom is established in the KJV: Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain" (Hebrew *yāda'*, H3045, "to know"). **[L3]** Genesis 24:16 defines a virgin in the same terms: "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." **[L2]** The Hebrew word behind the KJV's "virgin" is *'almāh* (H5959). **[L3]** Matthew 1:23 quotes it as fulfilled: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 shows that Mary's own report was that she had known no man. Luke 1:35 answers that report with the Holy Ghost coming upon her, not with a man. Isaiah 7:14 as quoted in Matthew 1:23 sets "virgin" together with "be with child." Mary's virginity at the conception, together with the stated divine source, leaves no place for a biological human father.

---

## 3. Joseph is not the biological father

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." **[L2]** *Apolusai* (G630), "to release, send away," is the word behind "put her away." **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

**[L4]** A husband who knew himself to be the father would have had no cause to be minded to put her away privily. Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph acting on the belief that the child was not his, and Matthew 1:20 resolves his fear by an angel's word that the child "is of the Holy Ghost," not of him.

**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." **[L2]** *Ouk eginōsken* ("he knew her not") is imperfect tense, a continued state, and it carries the same idiom of sexual knowledge. **[L3]** Genesis 4:1 gives the same use.

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543) means "was thought, was reckoned." **[L3]** John 6:42 records what the crowd said: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" **[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks the sonship to Joseph as an opinion held (*enomizeto*). John 6:42 shows who held it, namely the crowd, which is the same crowd the text records as contradicting him over where he came from.

**[L3] Luke 2:48–49:** Mary said, "Behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answered, "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" **[L4]** Mary's words use the ordinary household term (Luke 2:48). Jesus's reply redirects "father" to another (Luke 2:49). Together they show the household usage and the child's own claim standing side by side, which agrees with the supposed sonship of Luke 3:23.

---

## 4. The genealogy's grammar breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:2–16 the line runs on the active *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat," from father to son. At 1:16 the verb changes. It reads *ex hēs egennēthē Iēsous*, "out of whom [feminine singular] was born Jesus." The relative pronoun *hēs* is feminine, so it points to Mary and not to Joseph. The verb is passive, so Jesus is the one "born," not "begotten by" Joseph. **[L3]** Matthew 1:18 uses the same root, *genesis* (G1078), for "the birth of Jesus Christ."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2–16 uses "begat" for each father. At the last link, 1:16, the text puts Joseph as "the husband of Mary" and puts Jesus's birth "of whom" in the feminine. A text that kept the same verb for Joseph here would be making him the father. It does not.

---

## 5. A body prepared, and the woman's seed

**[L1] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." **[L2]** *Katērtisō* (G2675) means "to fit, to prepare." **[L3] Genesis 3:15:** "between thy seed and her seed." **[L2]** *Zera'* (H2233) means "seed." **[L4]** The seed spoken of in Genesis 3:15 is assigned to the woman. Hebrews 10:5 names the body as prepared (*katērtisō*) by God, and it is not said to have come from any man. Both verses fit the conception stated in Luke 1:35.

**Descent from David.** **[L1] Romans 1:3** says Christ was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L2]** *Sperma* (G4690) means "seed, offspring," and it names descent from David and not a father in the begetting. **[L3]** Luke 1:32 says of the child that "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." **[L4]** Davidic descent is attached to Mary by her own line and by the promise. Romans 1:3 and Luke 1:32 state that descent and do not name any begetter besides the Holy Ghost, so they stand with Luke 1:35.

[L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* and *ginōskō*; [L3] Matthew 1:16, 1:19, 1:25 and Luke 3:23; [L4] links 1–5 each exhibit two layers, and the text names a source, a virgin and a non-father without naming a human begetter.

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** I define "biological father" as a male who begets by his own seed. On the KJV's own words, Christ had none. His conception in Mary was "of the Holy Ghost", with no male begetter. [L4 on the verses below]

## 1. The conception is "of the Holy Ghost," before any union

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537 *ek*, "out of, from"; G4151 *pneuma*, "spirit"; G40 *hagios*, "holy"). The source of the conception is stated with *ek*, "out of".
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] *gennēthen* (G1080 *gennaō*, "to beget, to conceive") is the verb used of fathers begetting in Matthew 1:2. Here the begetting is said to be "in her" and "of the Holy Ghost".
[L3] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man... was minded to put her away privily." Joseph acts as a man who knows he is not the cause. He is reassured only by the angel's word in 1:20.
[L4] Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 both name the source as the Holy Ghost (*ek pneumatos*), and 1:18 places it "before they came together". Joseph's resolve in 1:19 fits only a man who knew the child was not his. So the source of the conception is not Joseph, nor any man.

## 2. Mary was a virgin, and Joseph "knew her not"

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L2] *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"), here of marital knowledge, in the present tense: Mary is not knowing a man.
[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
[L2] *episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") describes the power's act. *gennōmenon ek sou* (G1080, "born out of thee") names Mary alone as the source on the human side.

[L3] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son", quoted in Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
[L2] Hebrew *'almah* (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin". Greek *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") appears in Matthew 1:23 and in Luke 1:27.

A virgin who has not known a man has had no male begetter.

The child is David's seed "according to the flesh," out of the loins. "Of the Holy Ghost" marks the covenant origin of the child. It does not name a second begetter in place of the man the text names. [L4 on the chain below]

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whose seed a child is begotten. The question is whether Jesus Christ was begotten that way. My answer is no. The KJV gives his conception as "of the Holy Ghost" in a virgin. I do not deny that he is called the Son of God. I deny that a man begot him.

## 1. Matthew names the source of the conception, and it is not a man

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] In 1:18, "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905), "to come together", which here means the union of husband and wife. The pregnancy is dated before that union.
[L2] In 1:20, "conceived" is *gennaō* (G1080), "to beget, to conceive". The same verb is the "begat" of the genealogy. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from the source of". The begetting in her is therefore out of the Holy Ghost.
[L4] Footing: Matthew 1:18 puts the pregnancy before the union, and the verb and preposition of 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source. The only agent given for the begetting is the Holy Ghost, so no man begot him.

[L1] Luke 1:35 answers her: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
[L2] "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982), "to cast a shadow over". It describes God's power acting, not a man's.

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
[L2] The Hebrew is *'almah* (H5959), and the KJV renders it "virgin" here.

# CLOSE ROUND (DEFENDER)

I keep D1, D2, D3, D4 and D5 as declared. Nothing is conceded or narrowed. My chain rests on what the verses state. It does not rest on a demand that a verse state an exclusion.

## Answers on D1 (C4, C5)

- [L3] Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife." Deuteronomy 20:7 treats "betrothed a wife" and "taken her" as two steps.
- [L4] The child was already in her at the finding, and the finding is placed before any union (1:18). The only source Matthew attaches to that child is "of the Holy Ghost."
- The challenger says "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal." That cannot stand beside "before they came together" at the finding (1:18) and "knew her not" at the birth (1:25). No knowing is placed anywhere from the espousal to the birth.

The gate (22:24) threatens when another man is the source, so the angel's removal of the fear by naming the Holy Ghost as source meets exactly that danger.

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whose seed a child is begotten. The question is whether Jesus Christ was begotten that way. My answer is no. The KJV gives his conception as "of the Holy Ghost" in a virgin. I do not deny that he is called the Son of God. I deny that a man begot him.

## 1. Matthew names the source of the conception, and it is not a man

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] In 1:18, "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905), "to come together", which here means the union of husband and wife. The pregnancy is dated before that union.
[L2] In 1:20, "conceived" is *gennaō* (G1080), "to beget, to conceive". The same verb is the "begat" of the genealogy. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from the source of". The begetting in her is therefore out of the Holy Ghost.
[L4] Footing: Matthew 1:18 puts the pregnancy before the union, and the verb and preposition of 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source. The only agent given for the begetting is the Holy Ghost, so no man begot him.

## 2. Mary's question and the angel's answer

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."
[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L2] "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). [L3] Genesis 4:1 uses the same idiom: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived", where the Hebrew is *yada'* (H3045), "to know". Knowing a man is the way conception comes by a husband.
[L1] Luke 1:35 answers her: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
[L2] "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982), "to cast a shadow over". It describes God's power acting, not a man's.
[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
[L4] Footing: the "know" of Luke 1:34 is the "knew" of Genesis 4:1, and Luke 1:35 gives a different cause, the Holy Ghost, in answer to her "How?". Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" until the birth. The two accounts agree that no man's knowledge of her lies behind the conception.

## 3. The Scriptures foretold a conception by woman alone

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
[L2] The Hebrew is *'almah* (H5959), and the KJV renders it "virgin" here.
[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
[L2] The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin".
[L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed". The promised deliverer is called the woman's seed, with no man named.
[L3] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." The Greek *ginomai* (G1096) means "made, born".
[L3] Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me."

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whose seed a child is begotten. The question is whether Jesus Christ was begotten that way. My answer is no. The KJV gives his conception as "of the Holy Ghost" in a virgin. I do not deny that he is called the Son of God. I deny that a man begot him.

## 1. Matthew names the source of the conception, and it is not a man

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] In 1:18, "came together" is *sunerchomai* (G4905), "to come together", which here means the union of husband and wife. The pregnancy is dated before that union.
[L2] In 1:20, "conceived" is *gennaō* (G1080), "to beget, to conceive". The same verb is the "begat" of the genealogy. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), "out of, from the source of". The begetting in her is therefore out of the Holy Ghost.
[L4] Footing: Matthew 1:18 puts the pregnancy before the union, and the verb and preposition of 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source. The only agent given for the begetting is the Holy Ghost, so no man begot him.

## 2. Mary's question and the angel's answer

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."
[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L2] "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). [L3] Genesis 4:1 uses the same idiom: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived", where the Hebrew is *yada'* (H3045), "to know". Knowing a man is the way conception comes by a husband.
[L1] Luke 1:35 answers her: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
[L2] "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982), "to cast a shadow over". It describes God's power acting, not a man's.
[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
[L4] Footing: the "know" of Luke 1:34 is the "knew" of Genesis 4:1, and Luke 1:35 gives a different cause, the Holy Ghost, in answer to her "How?". Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" until the birth. The two accounts agree that no man's knowledge of her lies behind the conception.

## 3. The Scriptures foretold a conception by woman alone

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
[L2] The Hebrew is *'almah* (H5959), and the KJV renders it "virgin" here.
[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
[L2] The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin".

**My position.** The seed of David came "according to the flesh" out of a man's loins. The man the text names is Joseph, "of the house of David," the husband of Mary. "Of the Holy Ghost" marks the covenant origin of the child God claims as his son. It is not a begetting of flesh. I aim at the keystone **D5** and at the links it stands on, **D1** to **D4**.

[L4] Two footings support this. First, the oath names David's "bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12) and "loins" (Acts 2:30, *osphys*). Second, Hebrews 7:10 places a son "in the loins of his father." The promised flesh is therefore seed carried down a line of fathers out of David's loins. D5 sets "Of the Holy Ghost in a virgin" in the place of that line. The oath itself names David's loins as the source "according to the flesh."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L3] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me."
**[L2]** *Katartizō* (G2675) means "to fit, prepare, make ready." The body was made ready by God.
**[L3] Luke 24:39:** "a spirit hath not flesh and bones."
**[L4]** Luke 1:35 puts a causal "therefore" ("therefore also") between the Holy Ghost's coming and the title "Son of God." Hebrews 10:5 says the body was prepared, not begotten by a man. # OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:34 (Mary says she "know[s] not a man") and Genesis 4:1 (knowing leads to conception). The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 gives a conception without a man's knowing her. It does not correct her premise.

## 4. The angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means to overshadow. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the cause of the title "Son of God". The holy thing is "born of thee" (*ek sou*, out of you). Mary alone is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 repeats the same pairing: "of the Holy Ghost" for the conception, with "Mary thy wife" as the mother.

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:35 (*dio*, the Holy Ghost's coming as cause, and Mary as the one it is "born of") and Matthew 1:20 (the same two named). Together they give the whole account of the origin of the child. No third party, no human father, appears in either verse.

## 5. The prophecy foretold a virgin conception

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1] Matthew 1:22–23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet... Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959). It is a maiden of marriageable age, kept apart. The same word stands in Genesis 24:43 ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), where Genesis 24:16 says of the same girl that "neither had any man known her". Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), a virgin. The word is called a "sign", which marks it as something out of the ordinary.

**[L4]** The footing is Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh* as a virgin, called a sign) and Matthew 1:22–23 (the prophecy said to be fulfilled in this event, with *parthenos*). The prophecy was a conception by a virgin, fulfilled in Mary. A virgin who had a human father for her child would not have been a sign.

## 6. The people supposed Joseph the father, and the text says that was a supposition

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought or reckoned by custom". The text records a popular belief and marks it as only that.

**[L1] Luke 2:48–49:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Matthew 13:55 reports "Is not this the carpenter's son?"

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*, a supposition) and Luke 2:49 (Jesus, in answer to "thy father", points to "my Father's business"). The "father" language in John 6:42, Matthew 13:55 and Luke 2:48 reports what people said or assumed. The text itself marks that as supposition, and Jesus redirects the title to his Father in heaven.

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). # OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:34 (Mary says she "know[s] not a man") and Genesis 4:1 (knowing leads to conception). The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 gives a conception without a man's knowing her. It does not correct her premise.

## 4. The angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means to overshadow. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the cause of the title "Son of God". The holy thing is "born of thee" (*ek sou*, out of you). Mary alone is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 repeats the same pairing: "of the Holy Ghost" for the conception, with "Mary thy wife" as the mother.

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:35 (*dio*, the Holy Ghost's coming as cause, and Mary as the one it is "born of") and Matthew 1:20 (the same two named). Together they give the whole account of the origin of the child. No third party, no human father, appears in either verse.

## 5. The prophecy foretold a virgin conception

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1] Matthew 1:22–23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet... Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959). It is a maiden of marriageable age, kept apart. The same word stands in Genesis 24:43 ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), where Genesis 24:16 says of the same girl that "neither had any man known her". Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), a virgin. The word is called a "sign", which marks it as something out of the ordinary.

**[L4]** The footing is Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh* as a virgin, called a sign) and Matthew 1:22–23 (the prophecy said to be fulfilled in this event, with *parthenos*). The prophecy was a conception by a virgin, fulfilled in Mary. A virgin who had a human father for her child would not have been a sign.

## 6. The people supposed Joseph the father, and the text says that was a supposition

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought or reckoned by custom". The text records a popular belief and marks it as only that.

**[L1] Luke 2:48–49:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Matthew 13:55 reports "Is not this the carpenter's son?"

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*, a supposition) and Luke 2:49 (Jesus, in answer to "thy father", points to "my Father's business"). The "father" language in John 6:42, Matthew 13:55 and Luke 2:48 reports what people said or assumed. The text itself marks that as supposition, and Jesus redirects the title to his Father in heaven.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1] with *gennēthen ek* ("begotten out of", G1080/G1537) [L2] and Matthew 1:2 [L3] show that the conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost", before any coming together, using the same verb that elsewhere names a human father.

4. Luke 1:35 [L1] with *dio* ("therefore") and *episkiazō* ("overshadow") [L2] and Matthew 1:20 [L3] show that the angel names the Holy Ghost's coming as the cause of the conception, with Mary as the only human source.
5. Isaiah 7:14 [L1] with *ʿalmāh* (a virgin) [L2] and Matthew 1:22–23 [L3] show that a virgin's conception was foretold as a sign and is stated to be fulfilled in this birth.
6. Therefore, from links 1–5 [L4] together with Luke 3:23 [L1], *enomizeto* ("was supposed") [L2] and Luke 2:49 [L3], Christ had no human biological father. Joseph was husband and supposed father, and the conception was of the Holy Ghost.
