# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:34 (Mary says she "know[s] not a man") and Genesis 4:1 (knowing leads to conception). The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 gives a conception without a man's knowing her. It does not correct her premise.

## 4. The angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means to overshadow. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the cause of the title "Son of God". The holy thing is "born of thee" (*ek sou*, out of you). Mary alone is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 repeats the same pairing: "of the Holy Ghost" for the conception, with "Mary thy wife" as the mother.

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:35 (*dio*, the Holy Ghost's coming as cause, and Mary as the one it is "born of") and Matthew 1:20 (the same two named). Together they give the whole account of the origin of the child. No third party, no human father, appears in either verse.

## 5. The prophecy foretold a virgin conception

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1] Matthew 1:22–23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet... Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959). It is a maiden of marriageable age, kept apart. The same word stands in Genesis 24:43 ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), where Genesis 24:16 says of the same girl that "neither had any man known her". Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), a virgin. The word is called a "sign", which marks it as something out of the ordinary.

**[L4]** The footing is Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh* as a virgin, called a sign) and Matthew 1:22–23 (the prophecy said to be fulfilled in this event, with *parthenos*). The prophecy was a conception by a virgin, fulfilled in Mary. A virgin who had a human father for her child would not have been a sign.

## 6. The people supposed Joseph the father, and the text says that was a supposition

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought or reckoned by custom". The text records a popular belief and marks it as only that.

**[L1] Luke 2:48–49:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Matthew 13:55 reports "Is not this the carpenter's son?"

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*, a supposition) and Luke 2:49 (Jesus, in answer to "thy father", points to "my Father's business"). The "father" language in John 6:42, Matthew 13:55 and Luke 2:48 reports what people said or assumed. The text itself marks that as supposition, and Jesus redirects the title to his Father in heaven.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1] with *gennēthen ek* ("begotten out of", G1080/G1537) [L2] and Matthew 1:2 [L3] show that the conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost", before any coming together, using the same verb that elsewhere names a human father.
2. Matthew 1:16 [L1] with the feminine *hēs* ("of whom") [L2] and Matthew 1:25 [L3] show that the genealogy's "begat" pattern stops at Joseph and the birth is traced to Mary alone.
3. Luke 1:27 and 1:34 [L1] with *parthenos* (virgin) and *ginōskō* (to know) [L2] and Genesis 4:1 [L3] show that Mary was a virgin who had not known a man when the conception was announced.
4. Luke 1:35 [L1] with *dio* ("therefore") and *episkiazō* ("overshadow") [L2] and Matthew 1:20 [L3] show that the angel names the Holy Ghost's coming as the cause of the conception, with Mary as the only human source.
5. Isaiah 7:14 [L1] with *ʿalmāh* (a virgin) [L2] and Matthew 1:22–23 [L3] show that a virgin's conception was foretold as a sign and is stated to be fulfilled in this birth.
6. Therefore, from links 1–5 [L4] together with Luke 3:23 [L1], *enomizeto* ("was supposed") [L2] and Luke 2:49 [L3], Christ had no human biological father. Joseph was husband and supposed father, and the conception was of the Holy Ghost.

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:34 (Mary says she "know[s] not a man") and Genesis 4:1 (knowing leads to conception). The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 gives a conception without a man's knowing her. It does not correct her premise.

## 4. The angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means to overshadow. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the cause of the title "Son of God". The holy thing is "born of thee" (*ek sou*, out of you). Mary alone is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 repeats the same pairing: "of the Holy Ghost" for the conception, with "Mary thy wife" as the mother.

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:35 (*dio*, the Holy Ghost's coming as cause, and Mary as the one it is "born of") and Matthew 1:20 (the same two named). Together they give the whole account of the origin of the child. No third party, no human father, appears in either verse.

## 5. The prophecy foretold a virgin conception

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1] Matthew 1:22–23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet... Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959). It is a maiden of marriageable age, kept apart. The same word stands in Genesis 24:43 ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), where Genesis 24:16 says of the same girl that "neither had any man known her". Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), a virgin. The word is called a "sign", which marks it as something out of the ordinary.

**[L4]** The footing is Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh* as a virgin, called a sign) and Matthew 1:22–23 (the prophecy said to be fulfilled in this event, with *parthenos*). The prophecy was a conception by a virgin, fulfilled in Mary. A virgin who had a human father for her child would not have been a sign.

## 6. The people supposed Joseph the father, and the text says that was a supposition

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought or reckoned by custom". The text records a popular belief and marks it as only that.

**[L3]** John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Matthew 13:55 reports "Is not this the carpenter's son?"

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*, a supposition) and Luke 2:49 (Jesus, in answer to "thy father", points to "my Father's business"). The "father" language in John 6:42, Matthew 13:55 and Luke 2:48 reports what people said or assumed. The text itself marks that as supposition, and Jesus redirects the title to his Father in heaven.

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

Precept upon precept (Isaiah 28:10), the rows join without one being set against another:
- David's seed comes "out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12) and "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30).
- Joseph is "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4) and is "her husband" (Matthew 1:19).
- Mary calls him "thy father" (Luke 2:48).
- The canon's way of begetting is "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1).
- "Knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son" (Matthew 1:25) bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy after the taking.

So, at [L4] footed on these rows, Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal. # OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man by whom the child was begotten, the one who supplied the seed of conception. My position is that Jesus Christ had no such father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost while a virgin. Joseph was the husband and legal father only.

---

## 1. The conception is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** In Matthew 1:20, "conceived" is *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), meaning begotten or generated. "Of" is *ek* (G1537), meaning "out of", which names the source. The source of the begetting is the Holy Ghost. In Matthew 1:18, *synelthein* (from *synerchomai*, G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2 uses the same verb for ordinary fathers: "Abraham begat Isaac". The word names a human father in that case. In Matthew 1:20 the same verb names the Holy Ghost as source, and no man.

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:18 (found with child before any coming together), Matthew 1:20 (*gennēthen ek*, begotten out of the Holy Ghost) and Matthew 1:2 (the same verb naming a human father when one is meant). From these, the evangelist names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost where his own genealogy would name a man. No human begetter stands behind the conception.

## 2. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2–16 repeats *egennēsen* ("begat") for each father. At verse 16 the pattern changes. "Of whom" is *hēs*, a feminine singular relative pronoun. It points to Mary alone, not to Joseph. Joseph is *ton andra* ("the husband" or man) of Mary, and he is not said to have begotten Jesus.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". Luke 3:23 says Jesus was "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L4]** The footing is Matthew 1:16 with its feminine *hēs*, which breaks the repeated "begat" pattern, and Matthew 1:25, which says Joseph did not know Mary until the birth. From these, the Matthew genealogy gives a legal line through Joseph's name but marks, in its grammar, that the birth came from Mary alone.

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933) means a virgin. *Ginōskō* (G1097) in "I know not" means to know, and in this context it denotes marital intimacy. Mary's question assumes that a conception by ordinary means is not in view.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 uses the same sense: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:34 (Mary says she "know[s] not a man") and Genesis 4:1 (knowing leads to conception). The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 gives a conception without a man's knowing her. It does not correct her premise.

## 4. The angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (G1982) means to overshadow. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore") makes the Holy Ghost's coming the cause of the title "Son of God". The holy thing is "born of thee" (*ek sou*, out of you). Mary alone is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 repeats the same pairing: "of the Holy Ghost" for the conception, with "Mary thy wife" as the mother.

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 1:35 (*dio*, the Holy Ghost's coming as cause, and Mary as the one it is "born of") and Matthew 1:20 (the same two named). Together they give the whole account of the origin of the child. No third party, no human father, appears in either verse.

## 5. The prophecy foretold a virgin conception

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1] Matthew 1:22–23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet... Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *ʿalmāh* (H5959). It is a maiden of marriageable age, kept apart. The same word stands in Genesis 24:43 ("when the virgin cometh forth to draw water"), where Genesis 24:16 says of the same girl that "neither had any man known her". Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933), a virgin. The word is called a "sign", which marks it as something out of the ordinary.

**[L4]** The footing is Isaiah 7:14 (*ʿalmāh* as a virgin, called a sign) and Matthew 1:22–23 (the prophecy said to be fulfilled in this event, with *parthenos*). The prophecy was a conception by a virgin, fulfilled in Mary. A virgin who had a human father for her child would not have been a sign.

## 6. The people supposed Joseph the father, and the text says that was a supposition

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (from *nomizō*, G3543) means "was thought or reckoned by custom". The text records a popular belief and marks it as only that.

**[L1] Luke 2:48–49:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** John 6:42 reports the crowd: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Matthew 13:55 reports "Is not this the carpenter's son?"

**[L4]** The footing is Luke 3:23 (*enomizeto*, a supposition) and Luke 2:49 (Jesus, in answer to "thy father", points to "my Father's business"). The "father" language in John 6:42, Matthew 13:55 and Luke 2:48 reports what people said or assumed. The text itself marks that as supposition, and Jesus redirects the title to his Father in heaven.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition [L4].** By "biological father" I mean a man who begot the child. The standard reading says Jesus had no such man. His conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was father only by law and by supposition. The case rests on six blocks of text.

---

## 1. The conception is from the Holy Ghost, before any coming together

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek *synelthein* (συνελθεῖν, "to come together") sets the time of the conception before any union. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, "out of the Holy Spirit") names its source. *Ek* is the preposition of origin, "out of".

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel repeats the same source. The Greek *gennēthen* (γεννηθέν, "begotten, conceived") is the verb of begetting, and it is said of what is in her, with the Holy Ghost as its origin.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception before the union [L1, L2]. Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost, not Joseph, as the source of what was begotten in her [L3, L2]. So no man's act accounts for the conception.

## 2. Mary says she knows no man, and the angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (γινώσκω, "to know") is the word for sexual knowledge. *Andra* (ἄνδρα, "a man") is a male person.

**[L3] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The Hebrew *yada'* (ידע, "to know") is the same idiom. Matthew 1:25 uses it of Joseph: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (διὸ καί, "therefore also") makes the coming of the Holy Ghost and the overshadowing the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (ἐπισκιάζω, "to overshadow") is an act of power. It does not describe a man's act.

**[L4]** Mary asks how, with no man [L1, L2]. The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and it names no man [L1, L3]. The conception therefore has no male human contributor.

## 3. The genealogy changes its verb at the end

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac." The line continues with "begat" until **Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every man in the line is *egennēsen* (ἐγέννησεν, "begat", active). At the end the verb becomes *egennēthē* (ἐγεννήθη, "was born", passive). The relative *hēs* (ἧς, "of whom") is feminine singular, so it refers to Mary alone and cannot refer to Joseph.

**[L4]** The line says Joseph is "the husband of Mary" and says Jesus was born "of whom", that is, of her [L1, L2]. The unbroken "begat" pattern [L3: Matthew 1:2] stops before Jesus. The text did not credit Joseph with begetting him.

## 4. A virgin, as Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give it

**[L1] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Greek behind the KJV's "virgin" is *parthenos* (παρθένος, "virgin").

**[L3] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." The Hebrew behind it is *ha-'almah* (הָעַלְמָה, "the virgin"). The KJV renders the same Hebrew word as "virgin" in Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the conception before the coming together [L1]. Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give the sign as the virgin conceiving and bearing [L1, L3]. Together they say the conception happened while she was a virgin, so no man begat the child.

## 5. Joseph's conduct and role fit this

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

**[L4]** Joseph was minded to put her away, and the angel had to tell him the source [L1, L3]. A man who knew himself the father would have had no cause either to put her away or to be told. He did not believe himself the father until the angel told him otherwise.

**[L1] Matthew 1:21:** "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Kaleseis* (καλέσεις, "thou shalt call") gives Joseph the act of naming. A father by law names the child. The same verse says "she shall bring forth", which is her act.

**[L3] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." The Greek *katartizō* (καταρτίζω, "to prepare, fit") is the word for "prepared". The body was prepared by God. It was not begotten by a man.

## 6. The verses called "his father" and "the son of Joseph"

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (ἐνομίζετο, "was reckoned, was thought") is the verb of opinion, not of fact. The text itself marks the sonship as supposed.

**[L3] Luke 2:48:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers in Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" He corrects the use of "father" by pointing to a different father. **John 6:42:** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" These are the words of the speakers. The text reports them. It does not endorse them.

**[L4]** The speakers' usage in Luke 2:48 and John 6:42 [L3] is answered in the same chapters by Luke 3:23, where the text itself says "as was supposed" [L1, L2], and by Luke 2:49 [L3]. Those verses therefore do not show a biological father.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. The conception came from the Holy Ghost before any coming together. [L1] Matthew 1:18 "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost"; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* ("out of the Holy Spirit") names the source; [L3] Matthew 1:20 "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost".
2. Mary knew no man, and the angel named the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as the cause. [L1] Luke 1:34 "seeing I know not a man" and Luke 1:35 "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee"; [L2] *ginōskō* ("to know") and *dio kai* ("therefore also"); [L3] Genesis 4:1 "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived".
3. The genealogy gives Joseph the role of husband, not begetter. [L1] Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus"; [L2] *egennēsen* ("begat") changes to *egennēthē* ("was born") and *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine; [L3] Matthew 1:2 "Abraham begat Isaac".
4. The conception was by a virgin. [L1] Matthew 1:23 "a virgin shall be with child"; [L2] *parthenos* ("virgin") and *'almah* (the Hebrew word the KJV renders "virgin"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 "a virgin shall conceive" and Genesis 24:43 "the virgin cometh forth".
5. The "father" and "son of Joseph" verses express supposition and legal role, not begetting. [L1] Luke 3:23 "as was supposed the son of Joseph"; [L2] *enomizeto* ("was reckoned"); [L3] Matthew 1:21 "thou shalt call his name JESUS" and Luke 2:49 "my father's business".
6. Jesus had no biological father. A man begets, but Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source, Luke 1:34-35 excludes any man, and Matthew 1:16 does not credit Joseph with begetting him. [L1] Matthew 1:20, Luke 1:35; [L2] *gennēthen* ("conceived, begotten"), *ek* ("out of"); [L3] Matthew 1:16, Matthew 1:23.

# Defender, Round 2

The challenger's chain stands or falls on C5, that Joseph knew Mary before the child was conceived. I answer C5 first, then C1 to C4, then the presses. Every point carries its layers.

## A. C5 (keystone) is answered by Matthew 1:25, the challenger's own row

**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Heōs* (G2193, "until") with *ginōskō* (to know, as in Luke 1:34) gives the span: not knowing her from the taking-in until the birth. The challenger grants that *heōs hou* "bounds the abstaining to the pregnancy." The pregnancy begins at conception, so the abstaining covers the conceiving.

**[L3] Matthew 1:24:** "and took unto him his wife." **Matthew 1:18:** "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L4]** The challenger reads "came together" (1:18) as the taking-in of 1:24. Then the order is:
- Before the taking-in, she was already "found with child" (1:18) [L1, L3].
- From the taking-in until the birth, he "knew her not" (1:25) [L1, L2].

Under the challenger's own reading, 1:25 closes the window after 1:24, and 1:18 had already closed it before. Matthew 1:20 says the same: "that which is conceived in her", already conceived when the angel speaks to Joseph. Genesis 4:1 gives the ordinary means, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." In Matthew's account the knowing is placed after the birth ("knew her not till"), so the ordinary means is not what Matthew narrates. Deuteronomy 22:23-24 gives her status as "his neighbour's wife" if she were taken by another man. It gives no knowing by Joseph, while Matthew 1:25 states "knew her not till."

**Joseph's mind, Matthew 1:19-20.**

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L2]** *Boulomai* (G1014, "to be minded, to purpose") is his purpose on finding her with child.

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "But while he thought on these things... fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L4]** The challenger's own grounds for the intent are justice and mercy, and I grant them. The angel's *gar* ("for") then gives the ground for not fearing to take her: the child is "of the Holy Ghost." That ground answers what Joseph was thinking on, namely her being with child. The same verse says the child is of the Holy Ghost. If the angel meant a covenant claim over Joseph's own child, the ground would be no answer to Joseph's thought. His thought was that the child was not his. The verses give it as his thought, and the angel's "for" corrects it.

**[L4]** Joseph's house is the legal house into which the child was received by naming [L1, L3, L2]. The house reckoning in Numbers 1:2 therefore does not require Joseph to be the begetter.

## Hebrews 10:5

**[L1] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." **[L3] Hebrews 2:14:** "he also himself likewise took part of the same." **Hebrews 2:16:** "he took on him the seed of Abraham."

**[L2]** *Katartizō* ("to fit, prepare") is the verb behind "prepared"; its margin is "thou hast fitted me."

**Summary of where the chain stands.**
- Matthew 1:25 ("knew her not till") bars the challenger's keystone.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition [L4].** By "biological father" I mean a man who begot the child. The standard reading says Jesus had no such man. His conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was father only by law and by supposition. The case rests on six blocks of text.

---

## 1. The conception is from the Holy Ghost, before any coming together

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek *synelthein* (συνελθεῖν, "to come together") sets the time of the conception before any union. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, "out of the Holy Spirit") names its source. *Ek* is the preposition of origin, "out of".

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel repeats the same source. The Greek *gennēthen* (γεννηθέν, "begotten, conceived") is the verb of begetting, and it is said of what is in her, with the Holy Ghost as its origin.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception before the union [L1, L2]. Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost, not Joseph, as the source of what was begotten in her [L3, L2]. So no man's act accounts for the conception.

## 2. Mary says she knows no man, and the angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (γινώσκω, "to know") is the word for sexual knowledge. *Andra* (ἄνδρα, "a man") is a male person.

**[L3] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The Hebrew *yada'* (ידע, "to know") is the same idiom. Matthew 1:25 uses it of Joseph: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (διὸ καί, "therefore also") makes the coming of the Holy Ghost and the overshadowing the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (ἐπισκιάζω, "to overshadow") is an act of power. It does not describe a man's act.

**[L4]** Mary asks how, with no man [L1, L2]. The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and it names no man [L1, L3]. The conception therefore has no male human contributor.

## 3. The genealogy changes its verb at the end

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac." The line continues with "begat" until **Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every man in the line is *egennēsen* (ἐγέννησεν, "begat", active). At the end the verb becomes *egennēthē* (ἐγεννήθη, "was born", passive). The relative *hēs* (ἧς, "of whom") is feminine singular, so it refers to Mary alone and cannot refer to Joseph.

**[L4]** The line says Joseph is "the husband of Mary" and says Jesus was born "of whom", that is, of her [L1, L2]. The unbroken "begat" pattern [L3: Matthew 1:2] stops before Jesus. The text did not credit Joseph with begetting him.

## 4. A virgin, as Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give it

**[L1] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Greek behind the KJV's "virgin" is *parthenos* (παρθένος, "virgin").

**[L3] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." The Hebrew behind it is *ha-'almah* (הָעַלְמָה, "the virgin"). The KJV renders the same Hebrew word as "virgin" in Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the conception before the coming together [L1]. Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give the sign as the virgin conceiving and bearing [L1, L3]. Together they say the conception happened while she was a virgin, so no man begat the child.

## 5. Joseph's conduct and role fit this

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

**[L4]** Joseph was minded to put her away, and the angel had to tell him the source [L1, L3]. A man who knew himself the father would have had no cause either to put her away or to be told. He did not believe himself the father until the angel told him otherwise.

**[L1] Matthew 1:21:** "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Kaleseis* (καλέσεις, "thou shalt call") gives Joseph the act of naming. A father by law names the child. The same verse says "she shall bring forth", which is her act.

**[L3] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." The Greek *katartizō* (καταρτίζω, "to prepare, fit") is the word for "prepared". The body was prepared by God. It was not begotten by a man.

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (ἐνομίζετο, "was reckoned, was thought") is the verb of opinion, not of fact. The text itself marks the sonship as supposed.

A man begets, but Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source, Luke 1:34-35 excludes any man, and Matthew 1:16 does not credit Joseph with begetting him. # Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition [L4].** By "biological father" I mean a man who begot the child. The standard reading says Jesus had no such man. His conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was father only by law and by supposition. The case rests on six blocks of text.

---

## 1. The conception is from the Holy Ghost, before any coming together

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek *synelthein* (συνελθεῖν, "to come together") sets the time of the conception before any union. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, "out of the Holy Spirit") names its source. *Ek* is the preposition of origin, "out of".

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel repeats the same source. The Greek *gennēthen* (γεννηθέν, "begotten, conceived") is the verb of begetting, and it is said of what is in her, with the Holy Ghost as its origin.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception before the union [L1, L2]. Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost, not Joseph, as the source of what was begotten in her [L3, L2]. So no man's act accounts for the conception.

## 2. Mary says she knows no man, and the angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (γινώσκω, "to know") is the word for sexual knowledge. *Andra* (ἄνδρα, "a man") is a male person.

**[L3] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The Hebrew *yada'* (ידע, "to know") is the same idiom. Matthew 1:25 uses it of Joseph: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (διὸ καί, "therefore also") makes the coming of the Holy Ghost and the overshadowing the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (ἐπισκιάζω, "to overshadow") is an act of power. It does not describe a man's act.

**[L4]** Mary asks how, with no man [L1, L2]. The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and it names no man [L1, L3]. The conception therefore has no male human contributor.

## 3. The genealogy changes its verb at the end

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac." The line continues with "begat" until **Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every man in the line is *egennēsen* (ἐγέννησεν, "begat", active). At the end the verb becomes *egennēthē* (ἐγεννήθη, "was born", passive). The relative *hēs* (ἧς, "of whom") is feminine singular, so it refers to Mary alone and cannot refer to Joseph.

**[L4]** The line says Joseph is "the husband of Mary" and says Jesus was born "of whom", that is, of her [L1, L2]. The unbroken "begat" pattern [L3: Matthew 1:2] stops before Jesus. The text did not credit Joseph with begetting him.

## 4. A virgin, as Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give it

**[L1] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Greek behind the KJV's "virgin" is *parthenos* (παρθένος, "virgin").

**[L3] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." The Hebrew behind it is *ha-'almah* (הָעַלְמָה, "the virgin"). The KJV renders the same Hebrew word as "virgin" in Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the conception before the coming together [L1]. Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give the sign as the virgin conceiving and bearing [L1, L3]. Together they say the conception happened while she was a virgin, so no man begat the child.

**[L2]** *Kaleseis* (καλέσεις, "thou shalt call") gives Joseph the act of naming. A father by law names the child. The same verse says "she shall bring forth", which is her act.

# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition [L4].** By "biological father" I mean a man who begot the child. The standard reading says Jesus had no such man. His conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary, and Joseph was father only by law and by supposition. The case rests on six blocks of text.

---

## 1. The conception is from the Holy Ghost, before any coming together

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek *synelthein* (συνελθεῖν, "to come together") sets the time of the conception before any union. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου, "out of the Holy Spirit") names its source. *Ek* is the preposition of origin, "out of".

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel repeats the same source. The Greek *gennēthen* (γεννηθέν, "begotten, conceived") is the verb of begetting, and it is said of what is in her, with the Holy Ghost as its origin.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception before the union [L1, L2]. Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost, not Joseph, as the source of what was begotten in her [L3, L2]. So no man's act accounts for the conception.

## 2. Mary says she knows no man, and the angel names the cause

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (γινώσκω, "to know") is the word for sexual knowledge. *Andra* (ἄνδρα, "a man") is a male person.

**[L3] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The Hebrew *yada'* (ידע, "to know") is the same idiom. Matthew 1:25 uses it of Joseph: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (διὸ καί, "therefore also") makes the coming of the Holy Ghost and the overshadowing the ground of the child's being called the Son of God. *Episkiazō* (ἐπισκιάζω, "to overshadow") is an act of power. It does not describe a man's act.

**[L4]** Mary asks how, with no man [L1, L2]. The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and it names no man [L1, L3]. The conception therefore has no male human contributor.

## 3. The genealogy changes its verb at the end

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac." The line continues with "begat" until **Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every man in the line is *egennēsen* (ἐγέννησεν, "begat", active). At the end the verb becomes *egennēthē* (ἐγεννήθη, "was born", passive). The relative *hēs* (ἧς, "of whom") is feminine singular, so it refers to Mary alone and cannot refer to Joseph.

**[L4]** The line says Joseph is "the husband of Mary" and says Jesus was born "of whom", that is, of her [L1, L2]. The unbroken "begat" pattern [L3: Matthew 1:2] stops before Jesus. The text did not credit Joseph with begetting him.

## 4. A virgin, as Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give it

**[L1] Matthew 1:23:** "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Greek behind the KJV's "virgin" is *parthenos* (παρθένος, "virgin").

**[L3] Isaiah 7:14:** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." The Hebrew behind it is *ha-'almah* (הָעַלְמָה, "the virgin"). The KJV renders the same Hebrew word as "virgin" in Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the conception before the coming together [L1]. Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 give the sign as the virgin conceiving and bearing [L1, L3]. Together they say the conception happened while she was a virgin, so no man begat the child.

**[L3] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

**[L1] Matthew 1:21:** "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Kaleseis* (καλέσεις, "thou shalt call") gives Joseph the act of naming. A father by law names the child. The same verse says "she shall bring forth", which is her act.

**[L3] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me." The Greek *katartizō* (καταρτίζω, "to prepare, fit") is the word for "prepared". The body was prepared by God. It was not begotten by a man.

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (ἐνομίζετο, "was reckoned, was thought") is the verb of opinion, not of fact. The text itself marks the sonship as supposed.

The text reports them. It does not endorse them.

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position [L4]:** Jesus Christ had a mother, Mary, and no biological father. By "biological father" I mean a male who begets by seed. The KJV states that his conception was "of the Holy Ghost", with no man involved. Joseph was his father only by supposition and by law, not by begetting.

## 1. The conception is stated as having no human male cause

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek *synelthein* (G4905, "to come together") is used of the husband and wife coming together. The conception is placed before that point. *Ek pneumatos hagiou* means "out of the Holy Spirit", which names the source of the conception.

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Gennēthen* (G1080) is the passive of the verb for "beget" or "conceive". The text names the Holy Ghost as the source of what was begotten in her.

**[L3] Genesis 4:1:** "And Adam knew his wife; and she conceived." Here *yada* (H3045, "to know") comes before conception. The KJV treats conception as following a man's knowing of his wife.

**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:25 uses *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"), the word behind "knew" in Genesis 4:1 as the KJV carries it. Joseph did not know her until after the birth.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18, 1:20 and 1:25 give the source as the Holy Ghost, put the conception before coming together, and put Joseph's "knowing" after the birth. Genesis 4:1 shows the ordinary sequence, with knowing first and conceiving after. Here that sequence is absent, so no human male seed lies behind the child.

## 2. Mary's own words and the angel's answer

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") appears again. She is unknown by any man.

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* means "wherefore also" or "therefore". The Sonship title is given because of this conception.

**[L3] Luke 1:31:** "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son."

**[L4]** The question in Luke 1:34 is how she would conceive without knowing a man. The answer in Luke 1:35 names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. The answer fills the place a human father would have held.

## 3. The Holy Ghost is not a biological father

**[L1] Luke 24:39:** "for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have."

**[L2]** *Pneuma* (G4151, "spirit") is the word in Matthew 1:20 ("Holy Ghost" is *pneuma hagion*, "Holy Spirit").

**[L3] Hebrews 10:5:** "a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** *Katērtisō* (G2675, "to fit out" or "prepare") describes a body prepared, not seed received.

**[L4]** A spirit has no flesh, so the Holy Ghost cannot be a begetter of flesh by seed. Hebrews 10:5 describes the body as prepared. The Holy Ghost is the power that made the conception, not a male parent in the biological sense. Therefore the answer to the topic question is not "the Holy Ghost was the biological father". It is that no one was.

## 4. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern at the end

**[L1] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Through the whole list the verb is *egennēsen* (G1080), "begat". In verse 16 it changes to *egennēthē* (G1080), "was born", and the relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular. It points to Mary alone. Joseph is called "the husband of Mary", not the one who begat.

**[L4]** The pattern "X begat Y" runs unbroken to Joseph, and then stops. The line that was born is traced "of whom", meaning Mary. Matthew 1:16 grammatically denies Joseph the verb of begetting.

## 5. Joseph is "supposed" father, and the text says so

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543, *nomizō*, "to suppose" or "to reckon by custom") means thought to be so by common opinion, which is not the same as being so.

**[L1] Matthew 1:19:** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man... was minded to put her away privily."

**[L4]** A husband who knew himself to be the father would have had no cause to put her away. Joseph's resolve, set against the angel's word in Matthew 1:20 ("fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife"), shows he knew he was not.

**[L1] Luke 2:48:** "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**[L1] Luke 2:49:** "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?"

## 6. Scripture foretold this as a sign

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus was conceived in Mary without any man's begetting. Joseph was her husband and the child's legal and reputed father, not his biological father. By "biological father" I mean the man whose seed begets the child. The KJV assigns the conception to the Holy Ghost, and it says Mary had not been known by a man. Both points are built below from the text.

---

## 1. The genealogy changes its verb and its pronoun at the last step

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". The pattern of "begat" runs from verse 2 to verse 16.

**[L2]** The verb behind "begat" is *egennēsen*, from *gennaō* (G1080, to beget). In verse 16 the active verb gives way to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born". The relative pronoun is *hēs*, "of whom", which is feminine singular and so points to Mary alone. Joseph is called *anēr* (G435, husband), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 shows the pattern is "X begat Y". Matthew 1:16 drops that pattern for Joseph and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born. The author is steering the reader away from reading Joseph as the begetter.

---

## 2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Of" translates *ek* (G1537, out of, from a source). "Conceived" translates *gennēthen*, the passive of *gennaō* (G1080, to beget or conceive). This is the same verb the genealogy uses for "begat". The angel names the source of the begetting as *pneuma hagion*, the Holy Ghost, not a man.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982, to cast a shadow over, to envelop). "Therefore" is *dio kai*, "for which reason also".

**[L4]** Matthew 1:20 uses the begetting verb and gives its source as *ek pneumatos hagiou*. Luke 1:35 then ties the child's title "Son of God" to that act with "therefore also". The text puts the Holy Ghost, and no man, in the place of the begetter.

---

## 3. Mary had not been known by a man, and Joseph kept from her until the birth

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph".

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097), used here of marital knowledge. "Man" is *anēr* (G435). Mary's question assumes that without a man's knowing, there would be no conception. Luke 1:35 answers by naming the Holy Ghost instead.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** "Till" is *heōs hou* (G2193 with G3739, until which time). Joseph's not knowing her runs up to the birth.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:18 says she was found with child "before they came together". The conception therefore came before any union with Joseph.

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 shows Mary was not knowing a man. Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 place the conception before, and the non-knowing through to, the birth. The one natural channel of human fatherhood is excluded in the text.

---

## 4. The sign in Isaiah is of a woman who has not known a man

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son".

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *'almāh* (H5959). The Greek in Matthew 1:23 is *parthenos* (G3933, virgin).

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water". The Hebrew there is the same word *'almāh*. Genesis 24:16 describes the same woman as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** *'almāh* is used in Genesis 24:43 of a woman Genesis 24:16 states no man had known. The KJV therefore carries the sense of virgin in Isaiah 7:14. A sign that is "a sign" (Isaiah 7:14, "the Lord himself shall give you a sign") is a conception without the ordinary means.

---

## 5. Joseph was only the reputed father

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** "As was supposed" is *enomizeto*, from *nomizō* (G3543, to deem, to hold by custom or opinion). The text itself marks the sonship as an opinion held, not a fact of begetting.

**[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels Joseph's fatherhood "supposed". Luke 2:49 shows Jesus himself correcting it. ## 6. The body was prepared, not begotten by a man

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me".

**[L2]** "Prepared" is *katērtisō* (G2675, to fit, to make ready). The body is God's preparing.

**[L3]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Mary is the one who conceives, and the angel names no man as begetter.

**[L4]** Hebrews 10:5 names God as the one who prepared the body. Luke 1:31 names Mary as the one who conceived it. Luke 1:35 names the Holy Ghost as the power that came upon her. Together they leave no place for a human biological father.

6. Christ had no biological father. His body was prepared by God, conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man as begetter. [L1 Hebrews 10:5; L2 *katērtisō*; L3 Luke 1:31, Luke 1:35]

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus was conceived in Mary without any man's begetting. Joseph was her husband and the child's legal and reputed father, not his biological father. By "biological father" I mean the man whose seed begets the child. The KJV assigns the conception to the Holy Ghost, and it says Mary had not been known by a man. Both points are built below from the text.

---

## 1. The genealogy changes its verb and its pronoun at the last step

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". The pattern of "begat" runs from verse 2 to verse 16.

**[L2]** The verb behind "begat" is *egennēsen*, from *gennaō* (G1080, to beget). In verse 16 the active verb gives way to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born". The relative pronoun is *hēs*, "of whom", which is feminine singular and so points to Mary alone. Joseph is called *anēr* (G435, husband), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 shows the pattern is "X begat Y". Matthew 1:16 drops that pattern for Joseph and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born. The author is steering the reader away from reading Joseph as the begetter.

---

## 2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Of" translates *ek* (G1537, out of, from a source). "Conceived" translates *gennēthen*, the passive of *gennaō* (G1080, to beget or conceive). This is the same verb the genealogy uses for "begat". The angel names the source of the begetting as *pneuma hagion*, the Holy Ghost, not a man.

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982, to cast a shadow over, to envelop). "Therefore" is *dio kai*, "for which reason also".

**[L4]** Matthew 1:20 uses the begetting verb and gives its source as *ek pneumatos hagiou*. Luke 1:35 then ties the child's title "Son of God" to that act with "therefore also". The text puts the Holy Ghost, and no man, in the place of the begetter.

---

## 3. Mary had not been known by a man, and Joseph kept from her until the birth

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph".

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097), used here of marital knowledge. "Man" is *anēr* (G435). Mary's question assumes that without a man's knowing, there would be no conception. Luke 1:35 answers by naming the Holy Ghost instead.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** "Till" is *heōs hou* (G2193 with G3739, until which time). Joseph's not knowing her runs up to the birth.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:18 says she was found with child "before they came together". The conception therefore came before any union with Joseph.

**[L4]** Luke 1:34 shows Mary was not knowing a man. Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 place the conception before, and the non-knowing through to, the birth. The one natural channel of human fatherhood is excluded in the text.

---

## 4. The sign in Isaiah is of a woman who has not known a man

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son".

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *'almāh* (H5959). The Greek in Matthew 1:23 is *parthenos* (G3933, virgin).

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water". The Hebrew there is the same word *'almāh*. Genesis 24:16 describes the same woman as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** *'almāh* is used in Genesis 24:43 of a woman Genesis 24:16 states no man had known. The KJV therefore carries the sense of virgin in Isaiah 7:14. A sign that is "a sign" (Isaiah 7:14, "the Lord himself shall give you a sign") is a conception without the ordinary means.

---

## 5. Joseph was only the reputed father

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** "As was supposed" is *enomizeto*, from *nomizō* (G3543, to deem, to hold by custom or opinion). The text itself marks the sonship as an opinion held, not a fact of begetting.

**[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L3]** In Luke 2:48 Mary had said, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing". Jesus's reply in the next verse names a different Father.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 gives the reason he stopped: the angel said "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 labels Joseph's fatherhood "supposed". Luke 2:49 shows Jesus himself correcting it. Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph deciding to put Mary away, and he is turned back only by the angel's word in Matthew 1:20, not by his own fatherhood. Joseph's being called "father" is a matter of reputation and household standing, not begetting.

---

## 6. The body was prepared, not begotten by a man

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me".

**[L2]** "Prepared" is *katērtisō* (G2675, to fit, to make ready). The body is God's preparing.

**[L3]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Mary is the one who conceives, and the angel names no man as begetter.

**[L4]** Hebrews 10:5 names God as the one who prepared the body. Luke 1:31 names Mary as the one who conceived it. Luke 1:35 names the Holy Ghost as the power that came upon her. Together they leave no place for a human biological father.

---

6. Christ had no biological father. His body was prepared by God, conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man as begetter. [L1 Hebrews 10:5; L2 *katērtisō*; L3 Luke 1:31, Luke 1:35]

**Position.** [L4] Jesus was conceived in Mary without any man's begetting. Joseph was her husband and the child's legal and reputed father, not his biological father. ## 1. The genealogy changes its verb and its pronoun at the last step

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb behind "begat" is *egennēsen*, from *gennaō* (G1080, to beget). In verse 16 the active verb gives way to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born". The relative pronoun is *hēs*, "of whom", which is feminine singular and so points to Mary alone. Joseph is called *anēr* (G435, husband), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 shows the pattern is "X begat Y". Matthew 1:16 drops that pattern for Joseph and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born. The author is steering the reader away from reading Joseph as the begetter.

**[L2]** "Of" translates *ek* (G1537, out of, from a source). "Conceived" translates *gennēthen*, the passive of *gennaō* (G1080, to beget or conceive). This is the same verb the genealogy uses for "begat". The angel names the source of the begetting as *pneuma hagion*, the Holy Ghost, not a man.

**[L2]** "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982, to cast a shadow over, to envelop). "Therefore" is *dio kai*, "for which reason also".

**[L4]** Matthew 1:20 uses the begetting verb and gives its source as *ek pneumatos hagiou*. Luke 1:35 then ties the child's title "Son of God" to that act with "therefore also". The text puts the Holy Ghost, and no man, in the place of the begetter.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

## A. Hebrews 7:14: the defender's answer reckons within one seed

The defender answered with Genesis 48:5 and Deuteronomy 25:6.

[L1] Genesis 48:5: "thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt ... [are] mine."
[L3] Deuteronomy 25:6: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother [which is] dead."
[L2] Acts 2:30 "loins" is *osphys* (G3751, the loins, procreative power). Romans 1:3 "seed" is *sperma* (G4690, "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')").

[L4] Ephraim and Manasseh were born to Joseph, Jacob's son, so Jacob's reckoning in Genesis 48:5 moves inside Jacob's own seed. Deuteronomy 25:6 carries a dead man's *name* through a son begotten by the living brother. But the promise is set in seed, not name: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30), and "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3). A name-succession meets neither *osphys* nor *sperma kata sarka* ("seed according to the flesh"). So Hebrews 7:14's "sprang out of Juda" stands with Numbers 1:18's "by the house of their fathers": the descent ran through a father's house and loins, and that house is Joseph's, "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4).

**Position.** Christ had no human biological father. The KJV says Mary was a virgin and that "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20). It never names a man as the source of the conception.

---

## 1. Mary was a virgin when the child was conceived

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L2]** The word is *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin." Luke uses it twice in this one verse, and Matthew 1:23 uses it again.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097) means "to know," and here it means marital knowledge. *Anēr* (G435) means "a man, a husband." Mary's "I know not a man" is her stated reason why a conception seems impossible. The angel does not answer by naming a man.

**[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" is *ʿalmāh* (H5959), "a virgin of marriageable age." Genesis 24:43 uses the same word of Rebekah: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." Genesis 24:16 shows what the word covers: "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23 quotes the prophecy and applies it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L4]** From Luke 1:27 and 1:34 [L1], the Greek *parthenos* and *ginōskō* [L2], and Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23 [L3], I infer that the conception was announced to a woman who had known no man. A man's seed is therefore not the stated cause of the conception.

Therefore, the standard reading is fully sustained: Christ did not have a biological father.
